extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: LAMBADA is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.citeAs: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández. 2016. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv:1606.06031v1 [cs.CL]
extraction.rai:dataCollection: LAMBADA consists of passages composed of a context (on average 4.6 sentences) and a target sentence. The context size is the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens. The task is to guess the last word of the target sentence (the target word). The data come from the Book Corpus containing unpublished novels. The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The corpus contains unpublished novels and, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Passages were filtered to reduce time and cost of dataset collection by excluding passages that are relatively easy for standard language models. A combination of four language models was used: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model). Any passage whose target word had probability 0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The corpus was randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered using four language models to exclude relatively easy cases. The novels were pre-assigned to partitions to ensure passages are self-contained and cannot be solved by exploiting knowledge from the remainder of the novels. The same novel-based division method was used to further split LAMBADA data between development and testing.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A random sample of the remaining passages were evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: (1) one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if the guess was right, (2) a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if that guess was also right, (3) more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset. The subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence. It was ensured that the same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: two consecutive subjects were required to exactly match the missing word, and it was ensured that no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses. In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2 and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all the selection steps.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple annotations per item: 2 subjects for whole passage annotation (steps 1 and 2), and up to 10 subjects for sentence-only annotation (step 3), with 3 guesses allowed per subject in step 3
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models were used for filtering: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN), a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model trained on the Book Corpus
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The LAMBADA items contain quoted direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% of LAMBADA items vs. 61% of items in the input sample). More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. Most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and verbs (7.7%). Proper nouns are hugely over-represented in LAMBADA, while other categories are under-represented, compared to the POS distribution in the input.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset was designed to challenge language models with harder-than-average examples where broad context understanding is crucial. The constraint that the target word be the last word of the sentence makes the task more natural for human subjects but may introduce specific biases. The strict perfect-match approach (requiring exact word match rather than synonymous continuations) was chosen due to practical and methodological challenges in determining which alternative answers fit the passage well. Only 0.3% of target words are pronouns despite co-reference playing a big role. Verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are rare in LAMBADA, as many can be guessed with local sentence context only.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing. LAMBADA is meant to be used as a challenging test set to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task, specifically testing models' ability to take broad discourse context into account when predicting a word. The dataset is intended to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. Models should be trained on the provided training data (203 million words from 2,662 novels) and tested on the development and test sets.
